title: Double Electron Attachment and Double Ionization Potential Equation-of-Motion Coupled-Cluster Approaches with Full and Active-Space Treatments of 4-Particle-2-Hole and 4-Hole-2-Particle Excitations and Three-Body Clusters
comment: 15 pages and 4 tables. Supplementary Material as an ancillary file. This article has been accepted for publication in Chemical Physics Letters. After it is published, it will be found at
summary: The double electron attachment (DEA) and double ionization potential (DIP) equation-of-motion coupled-cluster (EOMCC) methods including up to 4-particle-2-hole (4$p$-2$h$) and 4-hole-2-particle (4$h$-2$p$) excitations on top of coupled-cluster singles, doubles, and triples (CCSDT), denoted DEA-EOMCCSDT(4$p$-2$h$) and DIP-EOMCCSDT(4$h$-2$p$), have been efficiently implemented in full and active-space forms. The resulting methods are applied to determine the ground and low-lying excited states of methylene, the singlet-triplet gap of trimethylenemethane, and the lowest singlet and triplet DIPs of 23 atoms and molecules. In all cases considered, the active-space DEA/DIP-EOMCC approaches recover the highly accurate parent DEA-EOMCCSDT(4$p$-2$h$)/DIP-EOMCCSDT(4$h$-2$p$) data at small fractions of the computational costs.

AI.tldr: Efficient implementations of DEA/DIP-EOMCC methods with up to 4p-2h/4h-2p excitations on top of CCSDT are presented, with active-space variants that recover full accuracy at reduced cost, validated on methylene, trimethylenemethane, and 23 atoms/molecules.
AI.motivation: To efficiently implement high-level DEA and DIP equation-of-motion coupled-cluster methods including up to 4-particle-2-hole (4p-2h) and 4-hole-2-particle (4h-2p) excitations on top of CCSDT, and to develop active-space approximations that reduce computational costs while preserving accuracy.
AI.method: Full and active-space implementations of DEA-EOMCCSDT(4p-2h) and DIP-EOMCCSDT(4h-2p) methods, applied to methylene, trimethylenemethane, and 23 atoms/molecules for benchmarking.
AI.result: Active-space DEA/DIP-EOMCC approaches recover the highly accurate full DEA-EOMCCSDT(4p-2h)/DIP-EOMCCSDT(4h-2p) data at small fractions of the computational costs.
AI.conclusion: The active-space implementations achieve near-exact agreement with full high-level methods while drastically reducing computational expense, making them practical for accurate double-electron attachment and double ionization potential calculations.

title: DynaMate2: Democratization of Agentic AI for Expert-Designed Custom Workflows
summary: Scientific workflows in computational chemistry and materials science typically involve multiple interdependent steps, such as model preparation, system construction, simulation execution, and data analysis, that researchers have refined over the years into highly specialized, validated codebases. While large language model (LLM) agent frameworks have demonstrated the potential to automate such workflows, existing systems are built for specific, pre-defined task sequences. Adapting them to new domains or integrating custom expert-developed tools requires substantial programming expertise, which limits their adoption across the broader scientific community. Here we present DynaMate2, a hierarchical agentic framework and open-source template whose central design goal is to lower the barrier for any researcher to convert their existing expert-defined Python functions into AI-callable tools within a supervised multi-agent pipeline. The key design principle is that the LLM is never asked to generate scientific code since all domain logic resides in expert-defined tools. The LLMs sole responsibility is to route tasks, select the appropriate tool, and use outputs to guide subsequent actions. Tools and agents can be registered at runtime from inline code, existing source files, or plain-language descriptions, and all extensions persist automatically across sessions. We demonstrate the framework through an end-to-end molecular dynamics workflow. We provide a Tool Registration Protocol that guides researchers step-by-step through the process of integrating their validated code into the framework. DynaMate2 is released as an open-source reference implementation with a web-based interface and is designed to serve as a reusable template for community-driven extension across arbitrary scientific domains.

AI.tldr: DynaMate2 is a hierarchical agentic framework that allows researchers to convert their existing expert-defined Python functions into AI-callable tools without writing scientific code, using LLMs only for task routing and tool selection. It supports runtime registration of tools/agents and persists extensions across sessions, demonstrated through an end-to-end molecular dynamics workflow.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent frameworks are built for specific, pre-defined task sequences and require substantial programming expertise to adapt to new domains or integrate custom expert-developed tools, limiting adoption across the broader scientific community. The goal is to lower the barrier for researchers to convert their validated codebases into AI-callable tools.
AI.method: DynaMate2 uses a hierarchical multi-agent pipeline where LLMs are restricted to task routing, tool selection, and output-guided decision-making—never scientific code generation. Tools and agents can be registered at runtime from inline code, source files, or plain-language descriptions, with automatic persistence across sessions. A Tool Registration Protocol guides integration step-by-step.
AI.result: Demonstrated through an end-to-end molecular dynamics workflow. The framework is released as an open-source reference implementation with a web-based interface, enabling community-driven extension across arbitrary scientific domains.
AI.conclusion: DynaMate2 successfully lowers the barrier for researchers to integrate expert-defined tools into an LLM-driven automation pipeline by confining LLM role to orchestration rather than code generation, and provides a reusable, extensible template for community adoption.

title: Information-Theoretic Appraisal of Electron Densities
summary: We present an information-theoretic assessment of atomic and molecular densities in the ground state and under a range of physical scenarios--excitation, confinement, and ensemblization. Comparisons across densities obtained from single-reference methods are facilitated through information entropy measures evaluated in position space. We demonstrate that the J-divergence serves as a key metric for benchmarking electron densities against coupled cluster and configuration interaction references. Mean-field orbital information is further compared with that of Brueckner and Dyson orbitals, and informational changes in multiple self-consistent-field solutions are examined under various symmetry-breaking conditions. We also explore the relationship between entropic measures of electron delocalization and the accuracy of the CO dipole moment computed with different methods. Our work offers insights into the selection of optimal reference determinants for a given chemical application and highlights potential benefits of incorporating information-entropy concepts in the development of new density functionals.

AI.tldr: This paper uses information entropy measures (especially J-divergence) to assess atomic and molecular densities from various single-reference methods, benchmarking them against coupled cluster and configuration interaction references. It also examines orbital information, symmetry-breaking in SCF solutions, and the link between entropic measures and accuracy of computed properties like the CO dipole moment.
AI.motivation: To provide an information-theoretic framework for assessing and benchmarking electron densities from different computational methods, enabling better selection of reference determinants and informing density functional development.
AI.method: Information entropy measures (including J-divergence) evaluated in position space; comparisons across densities from single-reference methods; benchmarking against coupled cluster and configuration interaction references; analysis of mean-field, Brueckner, and Dyson orbitals; examination of multiple SCF solutions under symmetry-breaking conditions.
AI.result: J-divergence is identified as a key metric for benchmarking electron densities. Entropic measures of electron delocalization correlate with accuracy of computed properties (e.g., CO dipole moment).
AI.conclusion: Information-entropy concepts can aid in selecting optimal reference determinants for chemical applications and may benefit the development of new density functionals.

title: Efficient purely organic phosphorescent emitters for programmable luminescent tags: from building blocks to donor-acceptor-donor structures
summary: Purely organic room-temperature phosphorescence (RTP) emitters are key components of programmable luminescent tags (PLTs), photonic devices for rewritable information storage and UV dosimetry. In this work, we systematically explore the design space of donor-acceptor and donor-acceptor-donor organic phosphorescent emitters in symmetric and asymmetric architectures. Phenoxathiine (PX) is introduced as an alternative donor to thianthrene (TA), combined with benzophenone (BP) or pyridine (Py) as acceptors. Through photophysical characterization, quantum chemical simulations, and PLT device testing, we identify structure-property relationships and, in particular, investigate the impact of the individual moieties on the emission properties and stability. The RTP emission wavelength is primarily tunable through the donor moiety: PX-based emitters emit sky-blue (λ_P = 480 nm), while TA-based emitters emit in the green (λ_P = 520 nm) due to an increased Stokes shift. The acceptor unit strongly influences the phosphorescence quantum yield, with Py-based emitters systematically outperforming BP-based ones. All newly synthesized PX-containing emitters show sufficient performance in PLT devices, though with reduced photostability compared to TA-based counterparts. Together, these results demonstrate that systematic donor-acceptor design enables predictable control over RTP emission properties, advancing the rational development of high-performance RTP-based photonic devices.

AI.tldr: This paper explores donor-acceptor and donor-acceptor-donor organic RTP emitters using phenoxathiine (PX) and thianthrene (TA) as donors with benzophenone (BP) or pyridine (Py) as acceptors, finding that donor moieties tune emission wavelength (sky-blue for PX, green for TA) and acceptor moieties influence quantum yield (Py outperforms BP), with overall structure-property relationships enabling predictable RTP emission control for photonic devices.
AI.motivation: To systematically investigate design space of donor-acceptor organic RTP emitters for programmable luminescent tags, rewritable information storage, and UV dosimetry applications.
AI.method: Systematic exploration of symmetric and asymmetric donor-acceptor and donor-acceptor-donor architectures; photophysical characterization; quantum chemical simulations; PLT device testing.
AI.result: PX-based emitters emit sky-blue (480 nm), TA-based emit green (520 nm); Py acceptors yield higher phosphorescence quantum yield than BP; PX emitters show sufficient PLT performance but reduced photostability compared to TA counterparts.
AI.conclusion: Systematic donor-acceptor design enables predictable control over RTP emission properties, advancing rational development of high-performance RTP-based photonic devices.

title: Lumina: An AI-Augmented Multiscale Material Informatics Framework for Extreme Aero-Chemo-Thermo-Mechanical Regimes
comment: This work was presented in High Energy Materials Conference & Exhibition 2026 and subsequently published in its proceedings
summary: Predictive simulations and experimental design involving extreme aero-chemo-thermo-mechanical regimes require high-fidelity material representation across diverse physical states. However, data for metals, polymers, and propellants, explosives, and pyrotechnics (PEP) remain fragmented, obstructing traceability for formulators, experimentalists, and simulation engineers. This work introduces Lumina, a modular Python-based informatics framework that centralizes multiscale material data from atomistic simulation datasets to macro-scale experimental records, within a unified repository. Lumina employs a hierarchical XML-based schema and a dynamic runtime parsing mechanism to enable schema-independent parameter extraction. Beyond storage, the platform provides computational modules to visualize model fits, allowing experimentalists to optimize design of experiments (DoE) and formulators to validate chemical behaviors against benchmarks. This structured architecture serves as a high-fidelity pipeline for training machine learning models and enhancing the accuracy of predictive simulations. To streamline multi-disciplinary workflows, Lumina integrates a conversational AI assistant for intelligent material retrieval and natural language querying. By consolidating multiscale data into an extensible ecosystem, Lumina provides a scalable foundation for data-driven discovery and predictive modeling in advanced defense and aerospace engineering.

AI.tldr: Lumina is a modular Python-based informatics framework that centralizes multiscale material data (from atomistic simulations to macro-scale experiments) into a unified repository using a hierarchical XML-based schema, with computational modules for visualization, machine learning pipeline support, and a conversational AI assistant for intelligent retrieval.
AI.motivation: Data for metals, polymers, and propellants/explosives/pyrotechnics (PEP) remain fragmented across different physical states, obstructing traceability for formulators, experimentalists, and simulation engineers in extreme aero-chemo-thermo-mechanical regimes.
AI.method: Lumina employs a hierarchical XML-based schema with dynamic runtime parsing for schema-independent parameter extraction; includes computational modules for model fit visualization and DoE optimization; integrates a conversational AI assistant for natural language querying.
AI.result: The framework enables centralized storage and retrieval of multiscale material data, supports experiment design optimization, validates chemical behaviors against benchmarks, and serves as a high-fidelity pipeline for ML model training.
AI.conclusion: Lumina provides a scalable, extensible ecosystem for data-driven discovery and predictive modeling in advanced defense and aerospace engineering by consolidating fragmented multiscale data.

title: Adaptive Multi-Fidelity Structural Optimization under Fluid-Structure Interaction
summary: The design of structures and vehicles subject to fluid-structure interaction (FSI) often requires high-fidelity coupled analysis. While the design variables pertain to the structure, the computational cost is dominated by the fluid solver, making iterative optimization prohibitively expensive. This paper presents an adaptive multi-fidelity optimization method combining high-fidelity FSI analysis with a lightweight surrogate for fluid-induced loads and a decision model that selects between surrogate and high-fidelity fluid evaluations. During optimization, completed FSI analyses incrementally update a non-intrusive surrogate model based on nearest-neighbor search and radial interpolation. A hybrid Lagrangian-Eulerian mapping function is developed to transfer fluid loads between structural designs. The evolution of surface orientation is handled by decomposing the traction vectors into local orthonormal bases. An adaptive Gaussian process regression model is employed to predict surrogate error and quantify uncertainty, allowing risk-aware selection of when coupled analysis is required. As design evaluations cluster near the optimum, the accuracy of the surrogate model naturally improves, thereby reducing the reliance on the fluid solver. It requires no offline training, preserves the high-fidelity structural model in all design evaluations, and ensures that the final design is evaluated by high-fidelity FSI analysis. The fundamental idea is justified theoretically using a simplified model problem, which shows that the leading-order error is a monotonically increasing, concave, and bounded function of the fluid added mass. The framework is demonstrated on two benchmark problems. For shape optimization of a flexible panel under shock loading, results show an $80\%$ reduction in computational cost while maintaining accuracy within $2.3\%$ of fully high-fidelity FSI optimization.

AI.tldr: An adaptive multi-fidelity optimization method for fluid-structure interaction problems that uses a surrogate model for fluid loads to reduce computational cost, achieving 80% cost reduction with under 2.3% accuracy loss.
AI.motivation: FSI optimization is dominated by expensive fluid solver costs, making iterative optimization prohibitively expensive. A method to reduce reliance on high-fidelity fluid evaluations while maintaining accuracy is needed.
AI.method: Combines high-fidelity FSI analysis with a lightweight surrogate for fluid-induced loads, using nearest-neighbor search and radial interpolation, a hybrid Lagrangian-Eulerian mapping for load transfer between designs, adaptive Gaussian process regression for surrogate error prediction, and risk-aware selection of when to use high-fidelity analysis.
AI.result: 80% reduction in computational cost while maintaining accuracy within 2.3% of fully high-fidelity FSI optimization on a flexible panel shape optimization benchmark under shock loading.
AI.conclusion: The method requires no offline training, preserves high-fidelity structural models in all evaluations, ensures final design is evaluated by high-fidelity FSI, and the leading-order error is a monotonically increasing, concave, bounded function of fluid added mass.

title: An AI-driven robotic system for two-dimensional hetero-assemblies
summary: Nanomaterials stacked on-demand, such as rotationally assembled two-dimensional (2D) van der Waals (vdW) layered compounds, provides a versatile platform for quantum simulation and the exploration of exotic electronic phases. Currently, however, such nanoassemblies remain largely confined to inefficiency, manually operated process, limiting their potential for probing emergent physical phenomena. There is a pressing need in the field for high-precision, automated assembling techniques, especially for the scalable fabrication of 2D twistronic heterostructures. Here, we present an intelligent automation system dedicated to the fabrication of van der Waals stacks, following the state-of-the-art protocol for dry transfer of exfoliated 2D materials. The system further employs metadata generated from each automated stacking procedure to perform reinforcement learning, thereby continuously bettering its performances. As a concrete demonstration, we fabricate twisted bilayer graphene (TBLG) -- known for its challenging preparation -- and exhibit its unconventional superconductivity near the magic angle. Our work may pave the way for high-throughput fabrication of low-dimensional nanomaterials including twistronic heterostructures, where integrating data mining and artificial intelligence can accelerate the discovery of novel physical phenomena.

AI.tldr: An intelligent automation system for fabricating van der Waals heterostructures uses reinforcement learning to improve its performance, demonstrated by successfully fabricating twisted bilayer graphene exhibiting unconventional superconductivity near the magic angle.
AI.motivation: Current nanoassembly of 2D van der Waals layered compounds is limited to inefficient, manually operated processes, which constrains the exploration of exotic electronic phases and the scalable fabrication of twistronic heterostructures.
AI.method: The authors developed an intelligent automation system following the dry transfer protocol for exfoliated 2D materials. The system uses metadata from each automated stacking procedure to perform reinforcement learning, continuously improving its performance over successive fabrication runs.
AI.result: The system successfully fabricated twisted bilayer graphene (TBLG) and demonstrated unconventional superconductivity near the magic angle.
AI.conclusion: This work paves the way for high-throughput, automated fabrication of low-dimensional nanomaterials and twistronic heterostructures, where integrating data mining and AI can accelerate the discovery of novel physical phenomena.

title: Targeting Clause Type Distributions: a Picklock for Random Satisfiability Problems
summary: Optimization problems such as the NP-complete 3-SAT provide an important benchmark for the difficult task of finding ground-states in strongly correlated many-body systems with rugged energy landscapes. The study of random 3-SAT problems as Ising spin Hamiltonians in statistical physics has yielded major insights including the existence of a satisfiability phase transition, and the prediction of a critical parameter line of particularly hard instances. Yet, progress on solving those instances has been scarce for several decades. Here, introducing the Target-SAT (TSAT) algorithm, we roughly triple the tractable problem sizes in the hardest regime, with an even greater improvement in a vast range of neighboring regions. By leveraging statistical information hidden in the combinatorial constraints of the problem, TSAT is actively guided in its stochastic local search toward a target within the relevant parameter space. Our analysis also explains why established local search algorithms are limited to relatively small system sizes due to a vast low-energy trap. Furthermore, we characterize the aforementioned critical line in terms of a dominant additional complexity barrier, whose exponential scaling is quickly overcome by TSAT only in the surrounding parameter space. With TSAT, the lead in solving the hardest known random satisfiability problems returns to the realm of stochastic local search algorithms.

AI.tldr: The TSAT algorithm roughly triples tractable problem sizes in the hardest 3-SAT regime by leveraging statistical information from combinatorial constraints to guide stochastic local search, overcoming low-energy traps that limit existing algorithms.
AI.motivation: Optimization problems like NP-complete 3-SAT serve as benchmarks for finding ground-states in many-body systems with rugged energy landscapes. Despite major insights from statistical physics (e.g., satisfiability phase transition, critical parameter line of hard instances), progress on solving those hard instances has been scarce for decades.
AI.method: Introduced Target-SAT (TSAT) algorithm, an actively guided stochastic local search that leverages statistical information hidden in combinatorial constraints to target relevant parameter space regions.
AI.result: TSAT roughly triples tractable problem sizes in the hardest regime with even greater improvement in neighboring regions. Analysis reveals why established local search algorithms are limited by a vast low-energy trap, and characterizes the critical line as a dominant complexity barrier with exponential scaling that TSAT overcomes in surrounding parameter space.
AI.conclusion: TSAT returns the lead in solving the hardest known random satisfiability problems to stochastic local search algorithms.

title: Spatio-spectral vector light created by optical activity in rubidium vapor
summary: We demonstrate a pump-probe scheme in which an atomic vapor is optically pumped with circularly polarized light and probed with a vector vortex beam. The pump induces a macroscopic magnetization in the medium, which gives rise to frequency-dependent circular dichroism and birefringence. The vortex probe, characterized by spatially varying polarization, maps this optical activity onto the spatial structure of the transmitted light, thereby generating correlations between the frequency, polarization, and spatial degrees of freedom. Measuring the intensity profile in a suitable polarization component then allows us to perform spatially resolved polarization spectroscopy. We demonstrate the translation of frequency shifts into an image rotation, observing on resonance a rotation in the order of 98 mrad per MHz. These findings may find applications in high-precision spectroscopy, magnetometry, and the generation of hybrid entanglement.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates a pump-probe scheme using atomic vapor pumped with circularly polarized light and probed with a vector vortex beam, enabling spatially resolved polarization spectroscopy through frequency-to-image rotation conversion (~98 mrad/MHz).
AI.motivation: To develop a technique that maps frequency-dependent optical activity (circular dichroism and birefringence) onto spatial structure of a vector vortex beam, enabling spatially resolved polarization spectroscopy with high precision.
AI.method: Atomic vapor is optically pumped with circularly polarized light to induce macroscopic magnetization, then probed with a vector vortex beam (spatially varying polarization). The pump-induced circular dichroism and birefringence create correlations between frequency, polarization, and spatial degrees of freedom. Spatially resolved polarization spectroscopy is performed by measuring intensity profiles in a selected polarization component.
AI.result: Frequency shifts are translated into image rotation, with an observed rotation of ~98 mrad per MHz on resonance.
AI.conclusion: The technique may find applications in high-precision spectroscopy, magnetometry, and generation of hybrid entanglement.

title: High Performance TiO2 Ferroelectric Field Effect Transistors with HfZrO2 for Neuromorphic Computing
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: TiO2 ferroelectric field effect transistors (FeFETs) with HfZrO2 (HZO) ferroelectric dielectric layers and bottom gate topology are fabricated for applications in neuromorphic systems. Two sets of devices are fabricated with different gate topologies by varying the thickness of the ferroelectric gate stack. Different device architectures are studied by varying the source drain length (LSD) and gate length (LG). The devices have high on/off ratios up to 10^7 with low leakage off currents <10^-12 A. Repeated cycle testing shows high reliability and a stable memory window. The devices have large memory windows ranging from 3 to 8 V.

AI.tldr: This paper presents TiO2 ferroelectric field effect transistors (FeFETs) with HfZrO2 (HZO) dielectric layers and bottom gate topology fabricated for neuromorphic systems. Two device sets with different gate topologies and varying ferroelectric gate stack thicknesses are studied, along with different source-drain (LSD) and gate lengths (LG). The devices achieve high on/off ratios up to 10^7, low leakage currents below 10^-12 A, high reliability with stable memory windows, and large memory windows ranging from 3 to 8 V.
AI.motivation: To develop TiO2 FeFETs with HZO ferroelectric layers for neuromorphic computing applications, exploring how different device architectures (gate topologies, thickness variations, and length scaling) affect performance.
AI.method: Two device sets with different gate topologies were fabricated by varying HZO ferroelectric gate stack thickness. Different architectures were studied by varying source-drain length (LSD) and gate length (LG). Devices used bottom gate topology with TiO2 channel and HfZrO2 ferroelectric dielectric.
AI.result: High on/off ratios up to 10^7, low leakage off currents below 10^-12 A, high reliability under repeated cycling with stable memory windows, and large memory windows ranging from 3 to 8 V.
AI.conclusion: The fabricated TiO2/HZO FeFETs demonstrate excellent electrical performance and reliability, making them promising candidates for neuromorphic system applications.

title: Representability-Aware Neural Networks for Reduced Density Matrices: Application to Fractional Chern Insulators
summary: We develop a representability-aware and interpolable neural network (NN) framework for predicting two-particle reduced density matrices (2-RDMs). The NN incorporates a subset of representability conditions through its architecture and loss function, and can operate on different momentum meshes, enabling evaluating the representability conditions across multiple meshes, which we call interpolated representability condition. The framework can be used either to predict 2-RDMs on large momentum meshes by interpolating exact results from small meshes, or as a variational 2-RDM ansatz optimized by energy minimization on arbitrary meshes. We apply this approach to the fractional Chern insulator in the one-band projected model of twisted bilayer MoTe$_2$ at twist angle $3.89^\circ$ and hole filling $2/3$. Trained on exact-diagonalization (ED) 2-RDMs from meshes with $12$ or $18$ momentum points using six different NN architectures, the best NN is the residual multilayer perceptron, which predicts the $6\times6$ 2-RDM with $97.07\%-98.18\%$ accuracy relative to the ED 2-RDM but predicts an energy $77.353$ meV above ED ground-state energy. We then variationally optimize the NN on several meshes including $6\times6$, predicting a $6\times 6$ energy of just $0.104$ meV below ED while maintaining $98.94\%-98.96\%$ accuracy. Compared with the conventional boundary-point semidefinite programming, which gives an energy $5.560$ meV below ED with $96.40\%-98.94\%$ accuracy, the NN achieves a more accurate energy and similar accuracy while using only less than 1/20 as many parameters. Eventually, we add a symmetric mesh of $48$ momentum points to the variational optimization of the NN, and provide a prediction of the many-body ground-state energy and the many-body quantum metric on that mesh.

AI.tldr: A representability-aware neural network framework predicts 2-RDMs with high accuracy on various momentum meshes, achieving variational energy minimization with far fewer parameters than conventional methods, and is applied to fractional Chern insulators in twisted bilayer MoTe₂.
AI.motivation: To develop a neural network framework that incorporates representability conditions for predicting 2-RDMs accurately and efficiently across different momentum meshes, enabling interpolation from small to large meshes and variational optimization for many-body quantum systems.
AI.method: A neural network framework is designed with representability conditions embedded in architecture and loss function, operating on different momentum meshes via interpolated representability conditions. Six NN architectures (best: residual MLP) are trained on ED 2-RDMs from 12- or 18-point meshes, then variationally optimized via energy minimization on meshes up to 6×6 (36 points) and a 48-point symmetric mesh, applied to the fractional Chern insulator in twisted bilayer MoTe₂ at 3.89° and 2/3 filling.
AI.result: Best NN predicts 6×6 2-RDM with 97.07%-98.18% accuracy (energy 77.353 meV above ED). Variational optimization achieves 0.104 meV below ED with 98.94%-98.96% accuracy (vs. boundary-point SDP: 5.560 meV below ED, 96.40%-98.94% accuracy), using <1/20 the parameters. Final prediction on 48-point mesh for ground-state energy and many-body quantum metric.
AI.conclusion: The representability-aware NN framework outperforms conventional SDP methods in energy accuracy and parameter efficiency, and enables scalable 2-RDM prediction on larger meshes beyond exact-diagonalization reach.

title: Random Matrix Spectra from Boltzmann-Weighted Lattice Ensembles
summary: We introduce a random matrix framework for studying statistical-mechanical lattice systems through spectral observables. Equilibrium configurations sampled from a Boltzmann measure are mapped to matrix ensembles whose covariance structure is inherited from the spatial correlations of the underlying model. This construction maps real-space correlation functions to a momentum-space variance profile, providing a direct bridge between statistical-mechanical correlations and correlated random matrix ensembles. We derive this variance profile in finite-correlation-length and critical regimes, and compute spectral moments within a Wick-contraction expansion. A complementary self-consistent description of the bulk density is developed using the resolvent formalism. These analytical methods are benchmarked against Monte Carlo data for the two-dimensional Ising model and three-dimensional Edwards--Anderson spin glasses. In both cases, the spectra evolve from the semicircle law at high temperature to model-dependent critical forms reflecting the structure of correlations. The framework, therefore, provides a quantitative spectral route to probing collective behavior in ordered and disordered statistical systems, while also defining a class of physically motivated correlated random matrix ensembles.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a random matrix framework to map equilibrium configurations of statistical-mechanical lattice systems (such as the Ising model and spin glasses) onto correlated matrix ensembles. The covariance structure inherits from spatial correlations, bridging real-space correlations to a momentum-space variance profile. Analytical methods (Wick-contraction, resolvent formalism) and Monte Carlo benchmarks show spectral evolution from the semicircle law at high temperature to critical forms reflecting correlation structure, providing a spectral route to probing collective behavior.
AI.motivation: To establish a direct spectral bridge between statistical-mechanical correlation functions and random matrix theory, enabling the use of spectral observables as probes of collective behavior in both ordered and disordered lattice systems, and to define physically motivated correlated random matrix ensembles.
AI.method: Equilibrium configurations from a Boltzmann measure are mapped to matrix ensembles with covariance inherited from spatial correlations. Real-space correlation functions are mapped to a momentum-space variance profile, derived in both finite-correlation-length and critical regimes. Spectral moments are computed via Wick-contraction expansion, and a self-consistent description of the bulk density is developed using the resolvent formalism. Validation is done against Monte Carlo data for the 2D Ising model and 3D Edwards–Anderson spin glasses.
AI.result: Spectra evolve from the semicircle law at high temperature to model-dependent critical forms that reflect the underlying correlation structure. The framework successfully reproduces and interprets spectral features in both ordered (Ising) and disordered (spin glass) systems, with analytical results matching Monte Carlo benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a quantitative spectral route to probing collective behavior in statistical systems and defines a class of physically motivated correlated random matrix ensembles, bridging statistical mechanics and random matrix theory.

title: Superconducting PdTe Thin Film Via Topotactic Transformation, Toward Topological Superconductors
comment: 14 pages, 4 figures, accepted for publication in ACS Applied Nano Materials
summary: Topological superconductors (TSCs) hosting Majorana zero modes (MZMs) offer a pathway to fault-tolerant quantum computation. PdTe is a promising TSC candidate due to its topological surface states and a reasonable superconducting critical temperature of ~4.5 K. However, it has been challenging to grow PdTe thin films with bulk-like superconducting properties. Here, we show that high-quality, superconducting PdTe thin films can be grown using molecular beam epitaxy (MBE). The films exhibit a sharp superconducting transition (T_onset = 4.43 K with transition width of 0.06 K), comparable to that of bulk crystals. This was made possible via a topotactic transformation from a PdTe_2 buffer layer to a PdTe phase by growing Pd on top under Te-deficient conditions. Structural and transport analyses confirm the NiAs-type structure of PdTe, as well as its two-dimensional superconducting behavior and excellent air stability. These findings suggest that the MBE-grown PdTe films and their heterostructures are a promising platform for topological superconductivity and Majorana physics.

AI.tldr: MBE-grown PdTe thin films exhibit bulk-like superconducting properties (Tc~4.43 K, ΔTc=0.06 K) via topotactic transformation from PdTe2 buffer, enabling a platform for topological superconductivity and Majorana zero modes.
AI.motivation: Topological superconductors hosting Majorana zero modes are promising for fault-tolerant quantum computation, but growing high-quality PdTe thin films with bulk-like superconducting properties has been challenging.
AI.method: PdTe thin films were grown by molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) via a topotactic transformation from a PdTe2 buffer layer by depositing Pd under Te-deficient conditions, followed by structural and transport characterization.
AI.result: The films show a sharp superconducting transition (T_onset = 4.43 K, ΔTc = 0.06 K), NiAs-type structure, two-dimensional superconducting behavior, and excellent air stability, with properties comparable to bulk crystals.
AI.conclusion: MBE-grown PdTe films with bulk-like superconductivity and air stability provide a promising platform for topological superconductivity and Majorana physics in heterostructures.

title: Modeling phase separation in polymer-derived carbonitride ceramics through extended machine learning molecular dynamics
summary: Polymer-derived ceramics combine the thermal stability of ceramics with the versatile properties of carbon domains, but modeling their atomic-scale evolution during processing remains elusive due to the limitations of traditional computational methods. To address this issue, here we develop and apply a machine learning interatomic potential for silicon carbonitride-based (Si-C-N-H) systems, trained on a diversified database of over 9000 configurations -including amorphous models, high-temperature states, surfaces, and crystal structure predictions - to capture the full complexity of these materials. This potential enables large-scale molecular dynamics simulations of 8000-atom systems revealing the atomic-scale evolution of the polymer-derived ceramic during thermal treatment. A key result of this work is the occurrence of a phase separation where carbon domains progressively nucleate from the amorphous SiCN matrix during thermal processing, forming distinct graphene-like sheets while preserving the integrity of the ceramic network. The resulting models reproduce the experimental atomic pair distribution functions with exceptional fidelity, validating our approach and providing microscopic explanations for the material unique combination of ceramic and graphitic properties. In this process, defective 5- and/or 7-member carbon rings, mediate the transformation to stable 6-member aromatic structures. These findings offer new atomic-scale insights into the thermal stability and structural transformation pathways of polymer-derived ceramics, while our methodology opens avenues for studying complex amorphous systems with first-principles accuracy at experimentally relevant scales.

AI.motivation: Modeling atomic-scale evolution of polymer-derived ceramics during processing remains elusive due to limitations of traditional computational methods; existing approaches cannot capture the full complexity of these materials.
AI.method: Developed a machine learning interatomic potential for Si-C-N-H systems trained on a diversified database of over 9000 configurations (amorphous models, high-temperature states, surfaces, crystal structure predictions), enabling large-scale molecular dynamics simulations of 8000-atom systems.

Defective 5- and 7-member carbon rings mediate the transformation to stable 6-member aromatic structures. Models reproduce experimental atomic pair distribution functions with exceptional fidelity.

title: Fröhlich-type Polarons in Isotopically Enriched Hexagonal Boron Nitride
comment: 34 pages, 6 figures, under review (supporting information is not included)
summary: Exciton-phonon interactions play a central role in defining the optical response of hexagonal boron nitride (hBN), yet their quantitative determination has remained incomplete. Here, we reveal the Fröhlich-type exciton-phonon coupling in boron-10-enriched hBN using low-temperature cathodoluminescence. We resolve the indirect exciton 5.95$\pm$0.02 eV together with its longitudinal optical (LO) phonon replica detuned by 184$\pm$56 meV, enabling the extraction of a Fröhlich coupling constant $α$=0.159 and a larger exciton binding energy of 161 meV, larger than previously reported values for natural-abundance hBN, which is attributed to isotope enrichment. The inferred polaron radius exceeds the lattice constant, indicating large-polaron behavior. We deduced an exciton scattering time ~of 97 fs, corresponding to a homogeneous linewidth of ~6.76 meV. We further obtain a polaron binding energy of ~48 meV and an effective mass of 1.045 $m_0$. These results provide a direct quantitative characterization of exciton-phonon coupling in isotopically engineered hBN and establish a foundation for tailoring its phonon-polaritonic and quantum-optical properties.

AI.motivation: Exciton-phonon interactions are central to hBN's optical response, yet their quantitative determination has remained incomplete.
AI.method: Low-temperature cathodoluminescence on boron-10-enriched hBN; resolved indirect exciton at 5.95±0.02 eV with LO phonon replica detuned by 184±56 meV.
AI.result: Fröhlich coupling constant α=0.159; exciton binding energy 161 meV (larger than natural-abundance hBN, attributed to isotope enrichment); polaron binding energy ~48 meV; effective mass 1.045 m₀; exciton scattering time ~97 fs (homogeneous linewidth ~6.76 meV); polaron radius exceeds lattice constant (large-polaron behavior).
AI.conclusion: Provides direct quantitative characterization of exciton-phonon coupling in isotopically engineered hBN, establishing a foundation for tailoring its phonon-polaritonic and quantum-optical properties.

title: Competing anisotropies and phase transitions in the $q$-state clock model with a $p$-fold crystalline field
summary: We study the two-dimensional $q$-state clock model in the presence of an additional $p$-fold symmetry-breaking crystalline field using Monte Carlo simulations. While the pure clock model exhibits Berezinskii--Kosterlitz--Thouless (BKT) transitions for sufficiently large $q$, the effect of competing discrete anisotropies on this topological phase remains nontrivial. We show that even weak crystalline fields qualitatively modify the phase diagram by suppressing the BKT phase and inducing transitions to states with true long-range order. The resulting behavior depends sensitively on the interplay between the intrinsic $\mathbb{Z}_q$ symmetry and the imposed $\mathbb{Z}_p$ anisotropy. In particular, in the six-state clock model for $p=2$ we observe qualitatively different scenarios depending on the sign of the field: a single transition for $h_2>0$ and a two-step ordering process for $h_2<0$ with an intermediate ordered phase. For $p=3$, the system exhibits a direct transition consistent with three-state Potts criticality. These results demonstrate that the phase structure cannot be inferred from symmetry considerations alone, but is governed by the competition between distinct locking mechanisms. Our findings provide a discrete counterpart to the multi-frequency sine-Gordon description of generalized $XY$ models and illustrate how additional anisotropies reshape topological phase transitions in two dimensions.

AI.tldr: Using Monte Carlo simulations, the paper studies the 2D q-state clock model with an additional p-fold crystalline field, finding that even weak discrete anisotropies suppress the BKT phase, induce true long-range order, and produce sign-dependent transitions (e.g., single vs. two-step ordering for p=2, three-state Potts criticality for p=3).
AI.motivation: To understand how competing discrete anisotropies (intrinsic Z_q symmetry and imposed Z_p crystalline field) modify the topological BKT phase in the 2D q-state clock model, going beyond pure symmetry considerations.
AI.method: Monte Carlo simulations of the two-dimensional q-state clock model with an additional p-fold symmetry-breaking crystalline field.
AI.result: Weak crystalline fields suppress the BKT phase and induce true long-range order. For q=6, p=2: a single transition for h_2>0, two-step ordering with an intermediate ordered phase for h_2<0. For p=3: direct transition consistent with three-state Potts criticality.
AI.conclusion: The phase structure is governed by competition between distinct locking mechanisms, not symmetry alone; the system serves as a discrete analog of multi-frequency sine-Gordon models for generalized XY systems.

title: Non-equilibrium exciton dynamics in tailored molecular potentials of Rydberg ion crystals
summary: Trapped ions excited to high-lying electronic states combine strongly coupled collective vibrational and electronic degrees of freedom with long-ranged interparticle interactions. These ingredients enable the quantum simulation of biochemical processes, associated with the dynamics of excitons in non-perturbative parameter regimes. The key feature of such a quantum simulator are electronic-state-dependent molecular potential surfaces which can be strongly coupled. This allows to shed light on a variety of mechanisms underlying exciton transport. We illustrate this in a system of three trapped ions, which is amenable to an ab initio treatment. Given that ion traps can be routinely prepared with hundreds of ions, these quantum simulators can immediately realise scenarios which are inaccessible by current numerical methods.

AI.tldr: Trapped ions in high-lying electronic states can simulate exciton dynamics in biochemical systems by combining collective vibrations, long-range interactions, and electronic-state-dependent molecular potential surfaces, offering insights into exciton transport mechanisms beyond classical computational reach.
AI.motivation: To enable quantum simulation of biochemical processes, specifically exciton transport dynamics, in non-perturbative parameter regimes that are inaccessible to classical numerical methods.
AI.method: Using trapped ions excited to high-lying electronic states, which feature strongly coupled collective vibrational and electronic degrees of freedom and long-range interparticle interactions. Electronic-state-dependent molecular potential surfaces serve as the key enabling mechanism. A three-ion system is treated ab initio as a proof of principle.
AI.result: Demonstration that a three-ion trapped-ion system can be treated from first principles, and the framework naturally extends to hundreds of ions, enabling simulations beyond current numerical capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Trapped-ion quantum simulators with high-lying electronic states can realize exciton transport scenarios that are currently inaccessible to classical computation, given that ion traps can routinely host hundreds of ions.

title: Ultrafast temperature diagnosis of dynamically compressed matter using millielectronvolt inelastic x-ray scattering beyond the first Brillouin zone
comment: 19 pages, 9 figures in main article; 2 pages, 1 figure in supplementary material
summary: We present calculations of the millielectronvolt-scale x-ray scattering spectra of multilayered dynamic-compression targets comprising an unstructured ablator layer and a crystalline, textured sample layer. Our model builds on the classic formulation of x-ray thermal diffuse scattering by Warren [B. E. Warren, Acta Crystallogr. 6, 803 (1953)] and includes both elastic and first-order (single-phonon) inelastic scattering contributions to the dynamic structure factor $S(\mathbf{q},ω)$. We focus on the umklapp scattering regime (i.e., at momentum transfers outside the first Brillouin zone) where the ablator scattering that threatens to overwhelm the inelastic scattering from the crystalline layer of interest is suppressed. We show that, despite the considerably more complex structure of the inelastic scattering spectra in this intermediate-$q$ regime, it is still possible to reliably deduce the temperature of the crystal using Dornheim's Laplace-transform--based formalism [Dornheim et al., Phys. Plasmas 30, 042707 (2023)], regardless of the details of the sample's texture.

AI.tldr: The paper presents calculations of meV-scale x-ray scattering from multilayered dynamic-compression targets, showing that crystal temperature can be reliably extracted using Laplace-transform-based analysis in the umklapp scattering regime despite complex spectral structure and ablator background.
AI.motivation: To enable temperature diagnosis of crystalline samples in dynamic-compression experiments by overcoming the challenge of ablator scattering that obscures inelastic signals from the sample layer.
AI.method: Builds on Warren's thermal diffuse scattering formalism, computes the dynamic structure factor including elastic and single-phonon inelastic contributions, and applies Dornheim's Laplace-transform-based formalism to extract temperature in the umklapp (intermediate-q) scattering regime.
AI.result: Despite more complex inelastic scattering spectra in the intermediate-q umklapp regime (outside first Brillouin zone), the temperature of the crystalline sample can be reliably deduced using the Laplace-transform approach, irrespective of sample texture details.
AI.conclusion: The umklapp scattering regime is a viable route for thermometry of crystalline samples in dynamic-compression experiments, with the Laplace-transform method robust to texture variations.

title: Textured phase diagrams of featureless insulators
summary: We study phase diagrams of charge-conserving `class A' non-interacting fermions, focusing on the trivial phase in various dimensions. Such phases are usually termed `featureless' to distinguish them from those others with either symmetry-broken or topological order. We show that the presence of non-trivial topological families of states, including charge pumps and their generalizations, results in phase diagrams being endowed with non-trivial topological textures that can be visualized through Berry phases and their higher-dimensional generalizations. We show that for non-interacting fermion systems with translation invariance, these `higher' Berry phases can be computed using integrals of non-abelian Chern-Simons forms of the Berry-Bloch connection over momentum and parameter spaces. Singularities in these textures correspond to gap-closing loci of `diabolical points', which represent the obstruction to contracting topologically non-trivial families of states, and bulk-boundary correspondence results in a locus of robust boundary modes that terminate at the bulk diabolical points. In the presence of finite chemical potential, we argue that the edge modes are generically robust without any need for fine-tuning for two and higher dimensions, whereas in one dimension they are `estranged' in the phase diagram, i.e. appearing at different parameter values for different edges. We demonstrate our results by constructing several microscopic models of non-interacting fermions. We argue stability to interactions and explore proximate phase diagrams by mapping to continuum field theories.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals that "featureless" trivial phases of non-interacting fermions actually possess non-trivial topological textures characterized by higher Berry phases and Chern-Simons forms, leading to robust boundary modes and diabolical points in the phase diagram.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that even trivial (featureless) phases of non-interacting fermions have rich topological structure beyond symmetry-breaking or topological order, arising from topological families of states like charge pumps.
AI.method: Uses Berry phases and higher-dimensional generalizations computed via integrals of non-abelian Chern-Simons forms of the Berry-Bloch connection over momentum and parameter spaces; constructs microscopic models and maps to continuum field theories.
AI.result: Phase diagrams exhibit non-trivial topological textures; singularities correspond to gap-closing diabolical points; bulk-boundary correspondence yields robust boundary modes terminating at bulk diabolical points; edge modes are generically robust in d≥2 with finite chemical potential, but "estranged" (appearing at different parameter values for different edges) in 1D.
AI.conclusion: Featureless phases are not truly featureless—they contain hidden topological structure; results are stable to interactions, and proximate phase diagrams can be explored via continuum field theories.

title: Dynamical systems on ultra small-world networks
summary: Despite the knowledge that social, economical, and ecological networks are often of a small-world nature with inter-nodal distance growing even slower than logarithmically with system size, we often assume theoretical systems to be outside of this regime, to make them easier to treat analytically. Here we derive a framework to apply the powerful dynamical mean-field theory on highly heterogeneous networks that is able to account for more of the degree correlations naturally arising from network constraints, known as structural cut-offs. We apply this framework to the well-studied and understood disordered Lotka-Volterra model, and show typically reported observables such as survival rates and stability for these systems on ultra small-world networks. We find much better agreement for these variables for all ranges of exponents for simulated power-law networks as well as empirically sourced networks.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a dynamical mean-field theory framework for highly heterogeneous networks that accounts for degree correlations from structural cut-offs. Applied to the Lotka-Volterra model on ultra-small-world networks, it shows improved agreement for survival rates and stability across power-law and empirical networks compared to standard approaches.
AI.motivation: Real-world networks (social, economic, ecological) are small-world with inter-nodal distance growing slower than logarithmically, yet theoretical models often ignore this regime for analytical tractability. The goal is to bridge this gap by accounting for degree correlations arising from network constraints (structural cut-offs).
AI.method: Derives a dynamical mean-field theory framework for highly heterogeneous networks that incorporates degree correlations from structural cut-offs, and applies it to the disordered Lotka-Volterra model on ultra-small-world networks.
AI.result: The framework yields much better agreement for survival rates and stability across all exponent ranges for simulated power-law networks and empirically sourced networks, compared to standard approaches that ignore the ultra-small-world regime.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for structural cut-offs and degree correlations in network dynamical mean-field theory significantly improves predictions for ecological dynamics on realistic small-world networks.

title: Pressure-induced superconductivity in epitaxially-stabilized Pr$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ films
summary: The discovery of high critical-temperature $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ superconductivity in La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ under high pressure has led to a rapid expansion of the $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ range through lanthanide $Ln$ substitution, and to ambient-pressure superconductivity in strained thin films, yet the exploration of new bilayer nickelates remains strongly constrained by thermodynamic stability. Beyond the difficulty of synthesis of bulk single-crystals, here we report on the pressure-induced high-$T_{\mathrm{c}}$ superconductivity in epitaxially-stabilized Pr$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ thin films. While the Pr$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ films exhibit insulating behaviour at ambient pressure regardless of ozone-annealing treatment, they show $T$-linear metallic transport and superconductivity reaching an onset $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ of 66 K and zero-resistance at nearly 40 K at 22 GPa. Furthermore, Nd$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$, with the smaller rare-earth ion Nd, can also be stabilized, however, superconductivity is not observed in the measured pressure range. Epitaxial stabilization enables us to examine the dependence of $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ and the critical pressure $P_{\mathrm{c}}$ for superconductivity on the $Ln$ ion in $Ln_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ ($Ln$ = La, Pr, Nd). These results suggest that a higher $P_{\mathrm{c}}$ is required for smaller $Ln$ ions, consistent with trends observed in bulk studies of $Ln$ substitution. This study demonstrates that epitaxial stabilization is a powerful technique to further expand the family of superconducting bilayer nickelates.

AI.tldr: This paper reports pressure-induced high-Tc superconductivity in epitaxially-stabilized Pr₃Ni₂O₇ thin films, with onset Tc of 66 K and zero-resistance at ~40 K under 22 GPa, while Nd₃Ni₂O₇ films do not show superconductivity. The study demonstrates epitaxial stabilization as a method to expand the family of superconducting bilayer nickelates and shows that smaller Ln ions require higher critical pressure for superconductivity.
AI.motivation: The exploration of new bilayer nickelate superconductors is strongly constrained by thermodynamic stability, making synthesis of bulk single-crystals difficult. The authors aim to overcome this limitation by using epitaxial stabilization to synthesize and investigate Pr₃Ni₂O₇ and Nd₃Ni₂O₇ thin films, expanding the family of superconducting bilayer nickelates.
AI.method: Epitaxially-stabilized Pr₃Ni₂O₇ and Nd₃Ni₂O₇ thin films were grown and characterized under high pressure (up to 22 GPa). Transport measurements were performed, including resistance vs. temperature at various pressures, with ozone-annealing treatment applied. The Ln ion dependence of Tc and critical pressure Pc was examined across Ln = La, Pr, Nd.
AI.result: Pr₃Ni₂O₇ films exhibit insulating behavior at ambient pressure but show T-linear metallic transport and superconductivity under 22 GPa, with onset Tc of 66 K and zero-resistance at ~40 K. Nd₃Ni₂O₇ films can be stabilized but do not show superconductivity in the measured pressure range. Smaller Ln ions require higher Pc for superconductivity, consistent with bulk studies.
AI.conclusion: Epitaxial stabilization is a powerful technique to expand the family of superconducting bilayer nickelates beyond thermodynamically stable bulk compounds. The study establishes a clear trend: smaller Ln ions demand higher critical pressure to induce superconductivity in Ln₃Ni₂O₇.

title: Dataset-aware entropy-maximized active learning for machine-learned interatomic potentials
summary: We present an active learning framework for efficiently generating training data for machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs). The method combines local entropy-driven molecular dynamics with global dataset-aware filtering: a per-configuration entropy term biases MD trajectories toward structurally diverse snapshots, while a global entropy measure, the log-determinant of the fingerprint covariance matrix of the entire dataset, selects only those configurations that provide genuinely new information. We employ dual covariance modes (per-atom for disordered structures and per-config for ordered phases) to achieve broad coverage of configuration space. Combined with a pre-trained foundation model (Allegro-OAM-L) and analytical fingerprint gradients from Gaussian overlap matrix eigenvalues, the framework produces high-quality domain-specific potentials with near- or sub-meV/atom accuracy on test data drawn from the same distribution at training-set sizes of order $10^{2}$ to $10^{3}$ entropy-selected DFT-labeled structures. We demonstrate the method on three systems spanning diverse bonding types and pressure-driven phase transitions: carbon (covalent), silicon (covalent/metallic), and NaCl (ionic). In learning curve comparisons against random molecular dynamics sampling at matched training set sizes ($N = 100$ to $800$), evaluated over three independent training-set draws per condition, entropy-driven sampling achieves a factor of approximately $3$ to $10$ lower energy MAE at $N = 800$ on in-distribution holdouts across the three systems, with the magnitude of the gain depending on the bonding type and the size at which the random-MD baseline saturates.

AI.tldr: Presents an active learning framework combining entropy-driven molecular dynamics with dataset-aware filtering to efficiently generate training data for machine-learned interatomic potentials, achieving 3-10x lower error than random sampling at matched training set sizes across carbon, silicon, and NaCl systems.
AI.motivation: To reduce the computational cost of generating training data for MLIPs by intelligently selecting the most informative configurations, rather than relying on brute-force random sampling or extensive DFT labeling.
AI.method: Combines local entropy-driven MD (biasing trajectories toward diverse snapshots) with global dataset-aware filtering (log-determinant of fingerprint covariance matrix). Uses dual covariance modes (per-atom for disordered, per-config for ordered phases) and a pre-trained foundation model (Allegro-OAM-L) with analytical fingerprint gradients from Gaussian overlap matrix eigenvalues.
AI.result: Entropy-driven sampling achieves factor of approximately 3 to 10 lower energy MAE at N=800 on in-distribution holdouts across carbon, silicon, and NaCl systems compared to random MD sampling, with near- or sub-meV/atom accuracy at training-set sizes of 10^2 to 10^3 entropy-selected DFT-labeled structures.
AI.conclusion: The framework produces high-quality domain-specific potentials efficiently, with the gain magnitude depending on bonding type and the size at which random-MD baseline saturates.

title: Topological phononics
summary: Topological phononics extends the foundational concepts of topological condensed matter physics to the realm of lattice vibrations and classical mechanical waves, unlocking robust, defect-immune states and phenomena beyond the reach of conventional phononic engineering. This review provides a unified, systematic framework for understanding topological phonons across natural and artificial systems, spanning solid-state materials, acoustic/mechanical metamaterials, and non-Hermitian platforms. We cover the core theoretical principles -- from Berry curvature and symmetry-protected topological invariants to bulk-boundary correspondence -- alongside experimental advances in probing topological phonon states via inelastic scattering and momentum-resolved techniques for solid-state phonons as well as pump-probe measurements in acoustic/mechanical metamaterials. Key topics include Weyl/Dirac/nodal-line phonons in crystalline solids, symmetry-engineered topological phases in metamaterials, non-Hermitian effects (exceptional points, skin effect), and emergent directions such as Floquet engineering, synthetic dimensions, and real-space topological textures (skyrmions, merons). We also highlight technological applications in robust waveguides, on-chip surface-acoustic-wave devices, and acoustofluidics, while outlining future challenges and opportunities in quantum phononics, nonlinear topological phenomena, and interdisciplinary integration with photonics and electronics. This review serves as a comprehensive guide across physics, materials science, and engineering, bridging fundamental theory with cutting-edge experiments and innovations in topological phononics.

AI.tldr: This review systematically covers topological phononics across natural and artificial systems, unifying theoretical principles (Berry curvature, topological invariants, bulk-boundary correspondence) with experimental advances and technological applications, while outlining future directions.
AI.motivation: Topological phononics extends topological condensed matter concepts to lattice vibrations and mechanical waves, enabling robust, defect-immune states beyond conventional phononic engineering, thus motivating a unified framework bridging theory, experiment, and applications.
AI.method: The review systematically integrates core theoretical principles (Berry curvature, symmetry-protected topological invariants, bulk-boundary correspondence) with experimental techniques (inelastic scattering, momentum-resolved methods, pump-probe measurements) across solid-state materials, acoustic/mechanical metamaterials, and non-Hermitian platforms.
AI.result: Key results include classification of Weyl/Dirac/nodal-line phonons, symmetry-engineered topological phases in metamaterials, non-Hermitian effects (exceptional points, skin effect), and emergent directions (Floquet engineering, synthetic dimensions, real-space topological textures such as skyrmions and merons).
AI.conclusion: Topological phononics demonstrates robust waveguides, on-chip SAW devices, and acoustofluidics applications, with future challenges and opportunities in quantum phononics, nonlinear topological phenomena, and interdisciplinary integration with photonics and electronics.

title: Excitation-Energy-Selective Control of Hot-Carrier Cooling via a Resonant Optical-Phonon Bottleneck in Graphene
summary: Understanding and controlling hot-carrier relaxation in graphene is crucial for advancing ultrafast optoelectronic and terahertz technologies. Here, we investigate carrier cooling dynamics in monolayer and bilayer graphene using mid-infrared pump pulses (0.22-0.73 eV) and terahertz probe pulses. We uncover a pronounced, reproducible, and non-monotonic dependence of the carrier relaxation time on excitation photon energy. Remarkably, within a narrow spectral window (0.42 to 0.48 eV), the carrier lifetime increases by an order of magnitude compared to a few picosecond-scale cooling observed at other energies. We show that this anomalous slowdown originates from a resonant enhancement of the optical-phonon lifetime, causing accumulation and reabsorption of hot optical phonons that suppress energy transfer to the lattice. All observed behaviors are captured within a unified carrier-phonon energy-balance framework, where excitation-energy-dependent variations of the effective optical-phonon decay pathway govern the cooling dynamics. These findings demonstrate excitation-energy-selective control of hot-carrier relaxation in graphene and provide new insight into non-equilibrium carrier-phonon interactions near the optical-phonon bottleneck.

AI.tldr: Carrier cooling in graphene shows a dramatic slowdown (10× longer lifetime) within a narrow photon energy window (0.42-0.48 eV), caused by resonant enhancement of optical-phonon lifetime that creates a hot-phonon bottleneck, fully captured by a unified carrier-phonon energy-balance model.
AI.motivation: Understanding and controlling hot-carrier relaxation in graphene is critical for advancing ultrafast optoelectronic and terahertz technologies.
AI.method: Mid-infrared pump pulses (0.22-0.73 eV) and terahertz probe pulses were used to investigate carrier cooling dynamics in monolayer and bilayer graphene.
AI.result: A non-monotonic dependence of carrier relaxation time on excitation photon energy was uncovered. Within 0.42-0.48 eV, carrier lifetime increases by an order of magnitude compared to the few-ps cooling at other energies, due to resonant enhancement of optical-phonon lifetime causing hot-phonon accumulation and reabsorption.
AI.conclusion: The findings demonstrate excitation-energy-selective control of hot-carrier relaxation in graphene and provide new insight into non-equilibrium carrier-phonon interactions near the optical-phonon bottleneck. All behaviors are captured by a unified carrier-phonon energy-balance framework.

title: Physical completion of the Navier-Stokes equations
summary: The incompressible Navier-Stokes equations contain viscous dissipation but no thermal noise. I show, using a topological argument based on Poincaré's lemma, that the fluctuation-dissipation relation for the full nonlinear dynamics can be derived without the linearisation or structural assumptions that all previous derivations require. The nonlinear convective term is Hamiltonian (energy-preserving and phase-space-volume-preserving) and drops out of the Fokker-Planck equilibrium condition exactly, so the noise derived from linearised fluctuations near equilibrium is in fact exact for the full nonlinear system. This result proves, rather than assumes, the reversible/irreversible decomposition that the GENERIC framework postulates, provided Poincaré's lemma holds on the phase space. The resulting stochastic system, with a physical molecular-scale spectral cutoff, is trivially globally well-posed: a finite-dimensional stochastic differential equation with non-degenerate noise and a confining Lyapunov function. It has a unique Gibbs equilibrium and converges to it exponentially. The difficulty of the Clay Millennium Prize Problem arises entirely from two idealisations, zero temperature and infinite spectral resolution, neither of which is satisfied by any physical fluid.

AI.tldr: The paper uses Poincaré's lemma to rigorously derive the fluctuation-dissipation relation for the full nonlinear Navier-Stokes equations without linearization, showing that the nonlinear convective term preserves energy/phase-space volume and drops out of the Fokker-Planck equilibrium condition. This proves the GENERIC decomposition axiom. With a physical spectral cutoff, the stochastic system is globally well-posed with unique Gibbs equilibrium and exponential convergence. The Clay Millennium Problem's difficulty arises from unrealistic idealizations (zero temperature, infinite resolution).
AI.motivation: To derive the fluctuation-dissipation relation for the full nonlinear Navier-Stokes equations without requiring linearization or structural assumptions, and to resolve the theoretical gap between deterministic Navier-Stokes and physically realistic stochastic fluid dynamics.
AI.method: Topological argument using Poincaré's lemma on the phase space; analysis of the Hamiltonian nature (energy-preserving and phase-space-volume-preserving) of the nonlinear convective term; showing exact cancellation in the Fokker-Planck equilibrium condition; introduction of a physical molecular-scale spectral cutoff to obtain a finite-dimensional SDE.
AI.result: The fluctuation-dissipation relation for the full nonlinear dynamics is exact without linearization; the GENERIC reversible/irreversible decomposition is proved rather than assumed; the resulting stochastic system with a spectral cutoff is globally well-posed with non-degenerate noise, a confining Lyapunov function, unique Gibbs equilibrium, and exponential convergence to equilibrium.
AI.conclusion: The Clay Millennium Prize Problem's difficulty stems from two physical idealizations (zero temperature and infinite spectral resolution) that no real fluid satisfies; the physically realistic stochastic formulation avoids these difficulties entirely.

title: Velocity collapse and non-conformal spiral phase in the sawtooth spin chain
summary: Recent matrix-product-state calculations show that the spiral phase in the sawtooth chain has numerical signatures that are difficult to reconcile with an ordinary conformal critical point: a large apparent central charge, slow dynamical scaling, nearly flat excitations, and no detectable dimerization. We develop a bosonization theory for this phenomenology by embedding the sawtooth limit in a zigzag ladder described by two coupled SU(2)$_1$ conformal field theories characterized by an extreme velocity ratio. We show that the sawtooth geometry cancels the leading staggered interaction, leaving a marginal twist interaction that selectively collapses the slow apical spin velocity. Crucially, as this velocity vanishes, the generated apical backscattering interaction diverges only in dimensionless units, causing the energy scale to collapse independently of the spatial correlation length. This mechanism naturally accounts for many of the numerical anomalies and we interpret the perturbative flow as an entrance to local quantum criticality in the strong-coupling regime.

AI.tldr: The paper explains numerical anomalies in the sawtooth chain's spiral phase (large central charge, slow dynamical scaling, flat excitations) by developing a bosonization theory that embeds the sawtooth in a zigzag ladder with two coupled SU(2)₁ CFTs. The sawtooth geometry cancels leading staggered interaction, leaving a marginal twist interaction that collapses the apical velocity, producing local quantum criticality.
AI.motivation: To resolve discrepancies between numerical signatures of the spiral phase in the sawtooth chain (large apparent central charge, slow dynamical scaling, nearly flat excitations, no detectable dimerization) and expectations for ordinary conformal critical points.
AI.method: Bosonization theory embedding the sawtooth limit in a zigzag ladder described by two coupled SU(2)₁ conformal field theories with an extreme velocity ratio; analysis of how the sawtooth geometry cancels the leading staggered interaction while leaving a marginal twist interaction that selectively collapses the slow apical spin velocity.
AI.result: The marginal twist interaction causes the apical backscattering interaction to diverge in dimensionless units as the apical velocity vanishes, leading to energy scale collapse independent of the spatial correlation length, which accounts for the observed numerical anomalies.
AI.conclusion: The perturbative flow is interpreted as an entrance to local quantum criticality in the strong-coupling regime, providing a theoretical framework for the unconventional numerical signatures observed.

title: Temperature-induced optical enhancement near a localization transition
summary: Quasiperiodic systems are an intermediate class of systems between periodic crystals and disordered systems, famously exhibiting metal-insulator transitions (MITs) even in one dimension. While their transport properties have been studied extensively, a systematic analysis of the finite-frequency optical conductivity near the critical point has been lacking. In this work, we carry out a detailed study of the optical conductivity in the paradigmatic Aubry-André model. We find that the zero-temperature low-frequency optical signal is strongly restructured by the quasiperiodic potential, exhibiting an optical gap that closes discontinuously as the system approaches the MIT. Most strikingly, we uncover a mechanism for a strong enhancement of the low-frequency finite temperature optical conductivity at certain resonant frequencies. This enhancement stems from the thermal activation of Pauli-blocked transitions between strongly resonant van Hove singularities. This mechanism provides new insight into finite-frequency transport in quasiperiodic systems and a new pathway for manipulating optical properties near a localization transition. Furthermore, our findings establish the optical response as a powerful, experimentally accessible tool for probing non-trivial quasiperiodicity effects.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the optical conductivity of the Aubry-André model near its metal-insulator transition, finding a discontinuous optical gap and a strong enhancement of low-frequency optical conductivity at finite temperatures due to thermal activation of Pauli-blocked transitions between van Hove singularities.
AI.motivation: A systematic analysis of finite-frequency optical conductivity near the critical point of quasiperiodic systems has been lacking, despite extensive studies of their transport properties.
AI.method: Detailed study of optical conductivity in the Aubry-André model, analyzing zero-temperature low-frequency optical signal, the behavior of the optical gap near the MIT, and finite-temperature effects.
AI.result: The optical gap closes discontinuously as the system approaches the MIT. A strong enhancement of low-frequency finite-temperature optical conductivity is found at resonant frequencies, arising from thermal activation of Pauli-blocked transitions between strongly resonant van Hove singularities.
AI.conclusion: The findings establish optical response as a powerful experimental tool for probing non-trivial quasiperiodicity effects and provide new insight into finite-frequency transport in quasiperiodic systems, as well as a pathway for manipulating optical properties near a localization transition.

title: Carrier-doping effect and anomalous transport properties in Ni-doped CeCoIn5 investigated by Hall resistivity measurements
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures, to appear in Phys. Rev. B
summary: We investigated the effects of Ni doping on carrier density and anomalous electrical transport properties in CeCo$_{1-x}$Ni$_x$In$_5$ ($x \leq 0.3$) by performing Hall resistivity measurements. The carrier density, estimated from the Hall coefficient $R_{\rm H}$ at a temperature of 0.5 K in high magnetic fields, increases linearly with $x$, indicating that the doped Ni ions act as electron dopants. In CeCoIn$_5$, the magnitude of $-R_{\rm H}$ is strongly enhanced at magnetic fields near the superconducting upper critical field $H_{c2}$ and in the low-field region above the superconducting transition temperature $T_c$. However, these anomalies are found to be significantly suppressed by Ni doping. Possible origins of this suppression in $-R_{\rm H}$ are discussed.

Ni acts as an electron dopant, linearly increasing carrier density. Anomalous Hall coefficient enhancements near $H_{c2}$ and above $T_c$ in CeCoIn$_5$ are significantly suppressed by Ni doping.

AI.method: Hall resistivity measurements performed on CeCo$_{1-x}$Ni$_x$In$_5$ ($x \leq 0.3$) at 0.5 K in high magnetic fields to extract carrier density from the Hall coefficient $R_{\rm H}$.
